title: The Japanese V-6 Engine So Reliable, The Automaker Still Hasn't Replaced It - Top Speed
content: Since Japan's introduction to the global automotive market, it has cemented a reputation for    creating engines that are efficient and reliable without sacrificing power. The industry achieved this by adopting traditional manufacturing philosophies that date back hundreds of years. This expertise came into play during its postwar industrial recovery, resulting in Japan becoming a global leader in powertrain engineering. Over the past 70 years, Japanese brands have refined a unique approach that combines extensive quality control with the     use of tried-and-tested technologies. In doing so, these brands ensure that performance gains never come at the expense of long-term durability. This engineering discipline was particularly evident as they expanded into the American premium market, where they introduced sophisticated six-cylinder engines aimed at competing with the region's heavier and less reliable V-8s. Honda is considered one of the leaders in this space, thanks to a well-balanced six-cylinder unit that remains in production today. After a successful initial run in the U.S., Honda began taking its approach to the American premium segment far more seriously. 1986 saw the introduction of the Acura sub-brand, which hit its stride during that same period and into the 1990s. "Precision Crafted Performance" was the primary ethos the brand applied to challenge far more established European and American segment leaders. Reliability and engineering acted as Honda and Acura's trump card, led by the Legend sedan and coupe. These premium midsize models quickly rose to become the best-selling luxury import in the United States for six consecutive years, spanning the late 1980s and early 1990s.     Acura followed this up with the NSX Benefiting from a lightweight, all-aluminum body and VTEC technology, it became an everyday supercar that could outperform the exotics of its era. Today, both Honda and Acura have pivoted toward crossovers and SUVs to align with market trends, but their ethos of doing more with less remains unchanged. In fact, many of the brand's powertrain foundations from the 1990s can still be seen in the vehicles they sell today. Honda's focus in the 1990s centered on powertrain mastery. The Japanese brand applied a philosophy that focused on extracting high power output from smaller-displacement units without sacrificing longevity. The brand achieved this by opting for aluminum components, including lightweight die-cast alloys for both blocks and heads to improve thermal efficiency and lower weight. A key design element was the refinement of variable valve timing and lift, which allowed engines to switch between distinct cam profiles. Honda's famous VTEC system This dual-mode capability optimized low-end fuel economy for daily commuting and high-RPM airflow for performance. It was supported by racing-derived innovations such as low-friction internal coatings, forged steel connecting rods, and high-precision secondary balancer shafts that virtually eliminated the vibrations inherent in inline four-cylinder designs. Honda went as far as developing its own specialized machining tools to achieve micron-level tolerances, cultivating a bulletproof reputation in the process. These engines were engineered to operate reliably at high rotational speeds that would have caused mechanical failure in many American and European rivals. Pick almost any random Honda on the road today, and you'll likely be met with a solid reliability projection. RepairPal ranks Honda number-one out of 32 car brands for reliability, with a 4.0 out of 5.0 rating. Both the frequency and severity of repairs related to Honda models are lower than the national average. Compared to Toyota — a historically reliable brand — Honda's brand-level costs and repair severity are lower. What this all means is Honda has obviously cracked the code for durable engineering. Taking a look at one of Honda's most reliable engines, the K-Series four-cylinder family, shows us just how far the brand's engineering has evolved, with multiple engines in the family easily achieving mileage in the 250,000 to 300,000-mile range with minimal maintenance requirements. But it's not the four-cylinder engine that has survived three decades, it's a more powerful sibling that occupies the V6 arena. And it does so without sacrificing what makes Honda engines so tough. The Japanese company first introduced this powertrain in the 1997 Acura CL, effectively debuting its J-Series V-6 family. This was Honda's official successor to the C-Series, maintaining a smooth 60-degree V-angle configuration. Its construction utilized a die-cast aluminum alloy block with iron cylinder liners for durability, paired with single overhead cam aluminum heads featuring four valves per cylinder. Honda also opted for a belt-driven valvetrain and a dual-stage intake manifold. Pairing this configuration with the VTEC system gave the engine a broad torque curve and high-RPM breathing capacity that rivaled larger-displacement engines in refinement. Reliability was a fundamental aspect of the development process, made possible by a forged steel crankshaft, high-strength connecting rods, and a simplified cooling circuit that reduced potential leak points. This robust approach to internal components means that the     J30 can easily surpass 200,000 miles with basic maintenance, setting a gold standard for the premium segment by offering a trouble-free ownership experience without sacrificing performance. Honda applied the J30 V-6 to several models that enjoyed considerable success in the U.S. market. The first vehicles to adopt it were the 1997 Acura 3.0CL and the 1998 Honda Accord V-6. Honda also used variations of this engine internationally in the Odyssey Prestige and Absolute trims, as well as the Honda Inspire and Avancier. Depending on the model, the J30 produces from 200 horsepower in the early J30A1 variants to a peak of 244 horsepower in the 30th Anniversary Edition J30A5. The torque range typically spans from 195 to 212 pound-feet. Honda typically mated these engines to four- or five-speed automatic transmissions paired with front-wheel drive, though the 2003 to 2007 Honda Accord V-6 Coupe was available with a six-speed manual transmission to appeal to driving enthusiasts. The engine's legacy was revived in a modernized, turbocharged form as the J30AC, which powered the now-defunct     Acura TLX Type S and continues to power the MDX Type S via a ten-speed automatic transmission and the brand's Super Handling All-Wheel Drive system, pushing outputs to 355 horsepower and 354 pound-feet of torque. According to Kelley Blue Book, keeping a J30-powered vehicle in peak condition requires strict adherence to its maintenance schedule. The most critical service is the timing belt and water pump replacement, typically recommended every 105,000 miles or seven years. Because this is an interference engine, a belt failure will cause the valves to strike the pistons, leading to catastrophic internal damage. Owners should also perform valve clearance adjustments every 105,000 miles — doing so ensures optimal engine breathing and prevents the ticking noise or burnt valves that can result from neglect. Routine oil changes should occur every 3,000 to 7,500 miles, depending on the oil type used, and transmission fluid replacements every 30,000 miles are standard. A full major service covering the timing belt, water pump, spark plugs, and coolant typically costs between $800 and $1,400, according to data from RepairPal, depending on local labor rates and whether OEM parts are used. While the J30's engine block itself is robust, models produced between 2001 and 2004 that were mated to the five-speed automatic transmission are notorious for overheating and internal clutch failure. On the engine side, common age-related issues include oil leaks from the VTEC spool valve or valve cover gaskets, EGR valve clogging that causes a rough idle, and cracked air intake boots that lead to vacuum leaks and lean engine codes. Of course, no engine is without its faults, and as reliable and proven as the J-Series engine family is, some variants are more renowned than others. Early J30-powered models — including the 1998–2002 Accord V-6, 1999–2003 Acura TL, 1999–2004 Honda Odyssey, and 2003–2008 Honda Pilot — have been reported to have more issues than later variants, including timing belt problems, oil leaks, excessive oil consumption, and occasional fuel injection and electrical quirks. For those shopping for used V-6 Hondas, a professional inspection should always come before any paperwork is signed. Owner forums and discussions on Reddit often point to the transmission as more of a problem area than the engine itself, with numerous owners reporting transmission problems around the 80,000 to 100,000-mile mark. Common issues include: The     modern state of the J-Series engine is characterized by a significant shift away from the traditional single overhead cam layout toward a more complex dual overhead cam configuration. Turbocharging is also a fundamental aspect of the engine's modernization, keeping it alive and relevant today. While the original J30 relied on a belt-driven valvetrain, today's flagship variants, such as the J30AC, adopt a twin-scroll turbocharger and a timing chain to produce more robust power and torque outputs. The latest naturally aspirated 3.5-liter J35Y8 variant powers the 2026 Honda Pilot and 2026 Honda Passport. This powerplant has also transitioned to a DOHC setup, producing 285 horsepower, with direct injection and a Variable Cylinder Management system designed to cut emissions. A ten-speed automatic remains the transmission of choice for these engines, available with either front-wheel drive or an advanced all-wheel drive system. Despite these advancements, the engine family maintains its signature 60-degree V-angle, which Honda insists is best for overall smoothness throughout the rev range. The brand has phased out the traditional VTEC engagement profile on these DOHC heads in favor of continuously variable timing control for more linear and efficient power delivery. Honda is currently facing backlash due to widespread V-6 engine failures among Honda and Acura models. Honda recalled over 200,000 V-6-powered models in 2023 due to a manufacturing defect involving the engine crankshaft, wherein the connecting rod bearings can prematurely wear and seize. Owners report unusual engine noises, misfires, power issues, stalled engines, and hesitation when accelerating. Affected models stretch all the way back to 2014. In January 2026, a lawsuit was filed stating that, despite the recall and subsequent remedy, Honda failed to address the underlying issues. Owners experiencing engine failure well before the 70,000-mile mark are being left to fend for themselves due to lapsed warranties, with some receiving repair quotes in the $10,000-plus range. While not all modern V-6 Honda and Acura models experience this issue, it has been widely reported and should be taken into account before purchasing. title: How V-BAT Earns Operational Trust - Shield AI
content: Our mission is to protect service members and civilians with intelligent systems. Two V-BATs sat on the deck aboard the Italian Coast Guard patrol vessel Dattilo, ready for a maritime surveillance mission run by Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency. Long before the aircraft reached Dattilo, Shield AI and Global Sat Tech, the operator, began working with the Italian Civil Aviation Authority (ENAC) to secure authorization for the mission. That authorization depended on more than the aircraft itself. ENAC evaluated the specific aircraft configuration, the crews, the operating procedures, and the mission plan. That process ultimately resulted in a Specific Assurance and Integrity Level III (SAIL III) authorization, the highest authorization to date in Europe for unmanned maritime operations. V-BAT brought an established operating record to the mission. It had already deployed aboard U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard vessels, flown in the Aegean, and operated daily in Ukraine against heavy electronic jamming. It was also in service with the Royal Netherlands Navy and under contract in Poland. Japan selected V-BAT as a maritime-based ISR platform, while India selected it for operations with the Indian Army. That operational record did not automatically authorize the mission aboard Dattilo. Before the mission could begin, the team had to demonstrate three things: Those three requirements are a big part of how V-BAT earns operational trust. The Dattilo mission shows how they come together in practice. Airworthiness is often described as whether an aircraft is safe to fly. This is accurate, but it also means something more specific: the aircraft operating in the field must be the same aircraft engineers designed, tested, and documented. The work starts before anything ships. Every V-BAT completes acceptance testing defined by our flight-test and engineering teams before delivery. Ground checks come first, followed by five flight-test cards with clear pass-or-fail criteria. No V-BAT leaves the factory until it completes all of them. The same discipline applies when the aircraft changes. Aircraft evolve throughout their service life. A customer may add a sensor that affects weight, power demand, or flight behavior. At our test ranges spanning the environmental envelope, our teams evaluate the modified aircraft, confirm that it performs as expected, and update the supporting manuals, procedures, training materials, and technical evidence before it reaches the customer. Documentation is not the end product or the goal. It is the record linking the aircraft in the field to the aircraft that engineers tested and validated. If the aircraft changes but its documentation does not, crews may follow procedures written for a different configuration, creating both a compliance gap and a safety risk. Airworthiness therefore does not end with a factory test or a single approval. It is the ongoing work of keeping the aircraft, its configuration, and the way crews operate it aligned throughout its service life. Mission readiness answers a different question: will it be ready when operators need it?  Reliability is one of the main drivers of that readiness. It begins with aircraft design, continues through production, and improves through operational experience. Design decisions can simplify maintenance, reduce failure points, and make it easier for crews to keep the aircraft flying over years of service. As an example, for the V-BAT Heavy Fuel Variant, we redesigned the electrical architecture and wiring harnesses, reducing the number of electrical connections on the aircraft. That means fewer potential failure points and fewer connections for maintainers to troubleshoot at 2 a.m. on a pitching deck. Those improvements add up. Across its operating life, V-BAT has maintained a mission-readiness rate above 98 percent. That level of readiness depends on more than engineering. It also takes people. Our field service representatives deploy alongside customers worldwide, working directly with operators and maintainers to troubleshoot issues, return aircraft to service, and bring lessons from the field back to our engineering and production teams in Texas. When crews identify an issue, it enters our safety management system, where it is assigned an owner and tracked through resolution. We like to think that the next crew inherits the fix, not the problem. An aircraft can be airworthy and mission-ready without being approved for every operation. Operational authorization applies to a specific operator, aircraft configuration, mission, and operating area – not simply to an aircraft model. That distinction is important because every mission presents different risks. An operation over open water differs from one near populated land. Launching from a moving patrol vessel introduces conditions that do not exist at a remote ground site. A different payload, flight path, or operating area can all change what an aviation authority needs to evaluate. The Dattilo mission illustrates how that process works. Shield AI worked closely with Global Sat Tech, Frontex, and the Italian Coast Guard throughout mission planning. Together, the teams documented the exact aircraft configuration, developed the concept of operations, and trained crews for normal, contingency, and emergency situations. Operational trust is built one mission at a time. Dattilo was one example. Shield AI has supported operators through mission approvals across North America, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific, working with military organizations and civil aviation authorities in a range of regulatory and operational environments. That experience helps us anticipate what different authorities require and prepare the documentation customers need to obtain authorization for their specific mission. ENAC assessed the proposed operation under the Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) framework used by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or EASA. Its review evaluated the operation as a whole: where and how V-BAT would fly, the risks to people, property, and other airspace users, and the procedures the operator would use to manage those risks. That process resulted in SAIL III authorization, the highest authorization level to date in Europe. The authorization showed that V-BAT’s safety case, operational procedures, and technical documentation met the requirements of an EASA Member State authority for beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) maritime UAS operations. Over 19 days, the two V-BATs flew day and night as a fully integrated part of the patrol vessel, logging 150 flight hours. At peak tempo, both aircraft were airborne simultaneously for a combined 20 hours a day and operated as far as 150 kilometers from the ship. They were also the largest unmanned aircraft in the 50-to-100-kilogram class that Frontex had flown from a On July 8, senior Frontex and Italian Coast Guard representatives watched a live search and rescue simulation in which one V-BAT located a small inflatable boat and helped coordinate the rescue. The aircraft matched the approved configuration, the crews followed the documented procedures, and the support team kept both V-BATs ready at the tempo the mission demanded. That preparation is what turned an authorization into 150 hours of operations at sea. It is the same work that helps customers and partners keep V-BAT flying critical missions around the world. Learn more about how we’re revolutionizing autonomy. Our mission is to protect service members and civilians with intelligent systems.

title: Fluminense v Palmeiras among lowest for ball-in-play under new rules - OneFootball
content: Get the full live experience with the OneFootball app. Fluminense’s 3-2 win over Palmeiras last Saturday (15) posted one of the lowest ball-in-play rates among the matches of the 23rd round of the Brazilian Championship, notably in the first round after the implementation of new rules aimed at fighting so-called “time-wasting” in Brazilian football. According to the data released after the round, the ball was in play for 51.9% of the time in the match between Fluminense and Palmeiras. That figure placed the game eighth in the ranking among the nine matches played in the round. Although it was below the weekend average, the rate in the Maracanã clash stands out when compared with the championship’s overall performance. Over the first 22 rounds, the average ball-in-play rate was 51.5%. In the 23rd round, that number jumped to 56.5%. In other words, even with one of the lowest rates of the round, the match between Fluminense and Palmeiras was still above the average recorded in the Brasileirão up to that point. The difference between the averages represents an increase of five percentage points in actual playing time. The rise comes right after the adoption of stricter measures to reduce delays in restarting play and other situations that contribute to reducing effective playing time in matches. The match with the highest percentage of ball in play in the round was Athletico-PR vs. RB Bragantino, at 62.1%. Next came São Paulo vs. Coritiba, at 59.8%, and Atlético-MG vs. Grêmio, along with Mirassol vs. Flamengo, both at 58.9%. Fluminense dominated possession and created more chances Even with the ball-in-play percentage below the round average, Fluminense managed to control much of the match against Palmeiras. The Tricolor finished the game with 60% possession, compared to the opponent’s 40%. The team also had the edge in attacking output. Fluminense had 17 shots to Palmeiras’ 15, in addition to six shots on target for each side. The team temporarily coached by Marcão also recorded four big chances, while the opponent had only one. Another stat that highlights the strong performance is the 2.18 expected goals (xG), compared to Palmeiras’ 1.10. Fluminense were also better in moving the ball: they made 487 passes, with 429 completed. Palmeiras finished with 317 passes, 261 of which reached their target. title: Bugatti Boss Mate Rimac Sure Sounds Like He Wants to Build a Stick-Shift V-16 Hypercar - Road & Track
content: It sure sounds like Bugatti’s CEO is thinking about cooking up a stick-shift hypercar. If you’re paying close attention, you might have noticed that manual transmissions are slowly creeping their way back into the supercar and hypercar world. And from the sound of it, Bugatti is certainly interested in jumping on the bandwagon. While speaking with Road & Track during Monterey Car Week, CEO Mate Rimac suggested a manual transmission is a real possibility for the future. When asked if there’s space for a Bugatti with a manual, Rimac emphatically said, “Yes, definitely. Definitely. I agree one hundred percent. Imagine [a] V-16 with a manual. Real manual.” While the V-16-powered Tourbillon was originally announced with an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic and no stick-shift option, this statement from Rimac sure makes it sound like Bugatti has its eyes on bringing a manual transmission into the fold. But the exact nature of any potential vehicle—whether it would be a one-off or part of the Tourbillon population—is what Rimac didn’t elaborate on. The Solitaire program could be an easier fit for such a project, as Bugatti’s one-of-one atelier is creating some incredible builds based on production vehicles. The first was Chiron-based, while another just shown at Monterey Car Week was based on the Bolide. As Bugatti begins introducing Tourbillon-based Solitaire projects to the world, doing a one-off manual would make for one hell of an entrance. (It would also be a touch disappointing if that was as far as it went, though; we’d love to see more than one three-pedal V-16 Bugatti roaming this earth.) One of the most telling parts of Rimac’s statement is that this gearbox would be a “real manual.” In other words, Bugatti seemingly has no intention to follow Ferrari down the path of the simulated manual transmission, the likes of which is being offered in the 12Cilindri Manuale. Any Bugatti manual will seemingly be the proper, real deal. We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we back.

title: How I Shot That: The Cameras Behind 18 Emmy-Nominated Series - IndieWire
content:

Happy Emmy voting week to all who celebrate and/or remember that there’s Emmy voting happening and use it as an excuse to catch up on some spring TV. As is tradition, the IndieWire Craft team reached out to all nominated cinematographers, regardless of category, to ask them about how they built the look of their shows. As is tradition, the answers are fascinating. There are a lot of returning veterans in the cinematography categories and a fair number of shows wrapping up their runs — someone else will have to light Jean Smart so damn alluringly now that “Hacks” is done; ditto the food on “The Bear.” In his answer to IndieWire, cinematographer Andrew Wehde described the FX show’s stalwart ALEXA Mini LF and Panavision H Series lenses as, “my only constant over the course of the series.” How shows either maintain or evolve their look over the course of a long run is a great problem for any cinematographer to have, and depending on the scope of the series, there are myriad different answers. Scott Duncan, one of the directors of photography on “Survivor,” told IndieWire about the ways in which the show has (over the course of 50 seasons, no less) improved its ability to execute cinematic compositions while furiously improvising on the sands of Fiji. “The question is always, ‘What can this tool give us that elevates the scene or story? It has to be functional, reliable, and most importantly, it has to add something to the visual language of ‘Survivor,'” Duncan said. But some very exciting new shows have entered the chat. Christian Sprenger has out-“Teddy Perkins”ed himself with the look of “Widow’s Bay,” and then elevated that look even further for the show’s Emmy-nominated episode, the flashback spooktacular, “Our History.” Changing the format, lenses, and aspect ratio, and leaning into a mostly handheld aesthetic in Episode 6, “shifted the feeling of the story while still maintaining the soul of the rest of the series,” Sprenger told IndieWire. Tackling a similar challenge, DP Gustav Danielsson needed to shift the existing visual vibes of Westeros to be more lived-in and down in the mud with the smallfolk of “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms.” There, the choice of lenses was about sculpting imagery that felt naturalistic without being too polished. “The Ultra Panatars helped us get that balance. They gave the images character without the anamorphic qualities becoming too obvious or distracting,” Danielsson said. Whether you’re looking to see how documentaries visually handle the passage of time or the depth of the oceans, whether you’re curious about how sitcom lighting informs camera setups, or whether you’d like to know how to make a Netflix show feel like “The French Connection,” these cinematographers found answers in the tools that they chose for the job. Nominated Episode: “Scallop” Dir: Christopher Storer; DP: Andrew Wehde Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour) Format: ARRIRAWCameras: ALEXA Mini LFLenses: Panavision H Series The Look: This has been the lens set and camera I have used since season 1 of ” The Bear.” If anything, they are my only constant over the course of the series. — Andrew Wehde Nominated Episode: “Isle of Joy” Dir: Justin Kurzel; DP: Pete Konczal, ASC Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited Or Anthology Series Or Movie Format: 8K RAW, 2.00:1 Aspect RatioCameras: Sony Venice 2Lenses: Leica R Primes, Leitz Hugo Primes, Angenieux Zooms, Leica ZoomsThe Look: We chose the 8K Sony Venice 2 not only for its low-light sensitivity, but also for how aggressive we could be in pushing the sensor. A low-contrast LUT was designed for the show that enabled us to get a very gritty, filmic look in both dark scenes and in broad daylight. To underscore the anxiety and emotion of the series, it was essential that the image felt dirty without breaking up. The deeper we went into the series, the more raw the light and lensing became. The Sony Venice was an incredibly versatile tool that was able to be pushed to extremes, just as the show’s two leads were. The Leica R and Leitz Hugo primes paired beautifully and have a unique street photographer’s quality that assisted in our observational approach. We were a longer lens show with much foreground. The 50mm, 75mm, and 90mm primes were exceptional in building layers while focusing the eye. Our Angenieux and Leica Zooms were detuned at TCS Camera in New York, where they added even more character and grit to the glass. We were very inspired by the tension created by slow zooms in 70’s films like “The French Connection.” The mix of primes and zooms helped us build an anxious world where we could keep the viewer off balance. — Pete Konczal Nominated Episode: “Destiny of the Republic” Dir: Matt Ross; DP: Adriano Goldman, ASC, BSC, ABC Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited Or Anthology Series or Movie Format: ARRIRAWCameras: ALEXA 35Lenses: Hawk Vintage 74 1.3x anamorphicThe Look: It’s a period show: the USA, late 19th century. I wanted to be able to rely on actual candles and oil lamps as much as I could, so I knew I was going to need high sensitivity on the sensors; we shot most of our interiors at 2560EI. It was also my first time working with Hawk lenses. The V74’s are really soft and beautiful; the anamorphic taste on a 2:1 aspect ratio gave me the intimacy I wanted for the characters, while also delivering epic wide vistas. The whole series was shot in Budapest, and we got the chance to work with an amazing Hungarian crew. — Adriano Goldman Nominated Episode: “Cornhole” Dir: Steve Conrad; DP: James Whitaker, ASC Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited or Anthology Series Or Movie Format: 6.5K ARRIRAWCameras: ALEXA 265 Lenses: Arri Prime DNA’s, assorted Vintage GlassThe Look: I wanted to focus on portraiture that felt like it was isolating characters within a frame in a meaningful way. The Alexa 265/ Prime DNA combo, with its stunning shallow depth of field and bokeh characteristics, helped me accomplish this goal in our photography. — James Whitaker Nominated Episode: “In God We Trust” Dir: Sam Levinson; DP: Marcell Rév Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (One Hour) Format: 65mm film, 35mm filmCameras: Arri 765, Arricam LTLenses: DNA primes, Panavision C-series and E-seriesThe Look: The 65mm format, in combination with the Verita film stock that Kodak developed for the show, gave us the resolution, saturation, and color separation that create a feel of richness and detail in the images we were trying to achieve for telling this story, while also preserving the organic feel and magic of celluloid that we love so much and keeping these tableaus grounded and realistic. — Marcell Rév Nomianted Episode: “It Will Stay This Way And You Will Obey” Dir: Jake Schreier; DP: James Laxton, ASC  Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited Series Or Anthology Series Or Movie Format: ARRIRAW Cameras: ALEXA 265Lenses: Arri 65 DNA The Look: I’ve always felt that the color science of Arri’s sensors gives beautiful skin tones and soft highlights with delicate shadows, so I knew we wanted to be in the Arri family. Our decision to use the Alexa 265 came from the feeling that our characters wanted to be symbols for the different generations that they represent, so giving the characters a different weight and scope from the 65-size format gave us that subtle feeling of emphasis that I was looking for. — James Laxton Nominated Episode: “The Garden” Dir: Lucia Aniello; DP: Adam Bricker, ASC Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour) Format: REDCODE RAW 8KCameras: V-RAPTOR XL [X] Lenses: Panavision Primo 70 The Look: Five seasons ago, we started “Hacks” on the Panavision DXL2 with RED’s MONSTRO sensor. Season after season, we’ve continued to evolve the camera system, ultimately finishing the series on the RED V-RAPTOR XL [X]. Each new generation of technology gave us an opportunity to improve both our images and our workflows, taking advantage of advances in dynamic range, wireless internal ND, and, ultimately, global shutter. The same is true of our lenses. Before the pilot, I worked with Panavision’s Guy McVicker to customize a set of Primo 70s specifically for “Hacks.” Over five seasons, Guy and I continued tinkering with that original recipe as the show evolved. I’ve loved that collaboration and the opportunity to spend six years refining a look. The real constant, though, has been our crew. So many of our key collaborators were there on the first day of the pilot and remained with us through the series finale. I’ve learned an enormous amount from them over these five seasons, and I’m thrilled to see their work recognized one last time. — Adam Bricker Nominated Episode: “In The Name of the Mother” Dir: Owen Harris; DP: Gustav Danielsson, FSF Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour) Format: ARRIRAW 4.5KCameras: ALEXA Mini LFLenses: Panavision Ultra Panatars Anamorphic 1.3 squeezeThe Look: I tested a huge number of lenses before deciding on the Panavision Ultra Panatar 1.3x anamorphic lenses for the show. I really liked the elegant and subtle anamorphic look of the Ultra Panatars. They’re sharp, but not too perfect. They’re large-format lenses, so we chose the ALEXA Mini LF because of its sensor size. The show’s aspect ratio was 2:1, so shooting ARRIRAW 4.5K 3:2 Open Gate meant we could use almost the whole sensor and not have to crop the image in post. I shot most of the show with the aperture almost wide open to get a shallow depth of field, only stopping down about half a stop to get the right amount of sharpness. The lenses were perfect for the look director Owen Harris and I wanted for the show. We wanted it to feel naturalistic and earthy, and beautiful without feeling too polished. “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” is a story about an ordinary hedge knight, Dunk, rather than kings and dragons, so we wanted Westeros to feel very real and lived-in. The Ultra Panatars helped us get that balance. They gave the images character without the anamorphic qualities becoming too obvious or distracting. Northern Ireland has an absolutely stunning landscape, and we tried to capture its earthy colors, together with all the mud, dirt, and textures of the world. I also knew that we would be shooting in every kind of weather. Northern Ireland is famous for getting four seasons in a day, so the ALEXA Mini LF was a great workhorse to rely on. Not only does it capture great images, but it also never fails to work. — Gustav Danielsson Nominated Episode: “Flamingos” Dir: Dearbhla Walsh; DP: Tari Segal, ASC Category: Outstanding Cinematography For A Series (One Hour) Format: 4.6k Apple ProRes 4444, 2.2:1 aspect ratioCameras: ALEXA 35Lenses: Panavision VA PrimesThe Look: Color was a huge part of the emotive progression of telling Margo’s story. The ALEXA 35 really excels in capturing natural skin tones while also reproducing the broad range of colors we added on set through our lighting. Carl Herse brought on the VA primes, which proved to be a beautiful pairing to the ALEXA 35. They have a very natural softness to them and an organic bokeh that helped layer realism to a vibrant show. Their compact and lightweight nature also helped us when designing complex shots when space was limited and when we shot with our babies. — Tari Segal Dir: Mariska Hargitay, DP: Tony HardmonCategory: Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program Format: 4K Full Frame, 2:1 Aspect ratio, SLog3-CineCameras: Sony FX9Lenses: Cooke Panchro/iClassics FF and the Angenieux EZ1 FF 45mm-135mmThe Look: “My Mom Jayne” documents Mariska Hargitay’s search to discover the true story of her mother, Hollywood actress Jayne Mansfield, who died in a car crash when Mariska was just three years old. The intention of our visual language was to connect Mariska and her family to the extensive archival footage of her mother, Jayne. The interviews were shot with Sony FX9s, paired with Cooke Panchro/iClassic full-frame primes. The vintage softness and fall off of the Cookes was a nod to the glamorous 50’s and 60’s movie eras of Jayne Mansfield’s time. Mitchell ‘D’ soft diffusion filters complemented the throwback look. Documenting Mariska’s family required a delicate and respectful approach. I’d previously collaborated with Mariska and Producer Trish Adlesic on the documentary “I Am Evidence,” so I had insight into the warm, conversational, and intimate filmmaking style they desired. I kept the set environment quiet and unhurried, so all involved had the time and space to sit with the memories that were still very painful to speak aloud. Verite scenes were shot single-camera, pairing the Sony FX9 with the Angenieux EZ1 in full frame, 45mm-135mm. The FX9 verite build allowed me to capture spontaneous moments of revelation as Mariska discovered her mother in real time. — Tony Hardmon Dir: Colin Butfield, Toby Nowlan, Keith Scholey; DPs: Doug Anderson, Toby StrongCategory: Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program Format: RedcodeCameras: Red Raptor 8K VVLenses: NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S – NIKKOR Z 24-70mm f/2.8 S – AF Zoom-Nikkor 70-180mm f/4.5-5.6D ED Micro (the classic F-mount macro zoom) – Laowa 24mm f/14 Probe Lens (Venus Optics) – Canon MP-E 65mm f/2.8 1-5x Macro Photo – Infinity Photo-Optical InfiniProbe TS-160 ROBUSTO™The Look: For me, image quality is everything. Underwater, every additional centimetre of water between the lens and the subject reduces contrast, colour and apparent sharpness. The NIKKOR Z 14–24mm f/2.8 S produces exceptional edge-to-edge sharpness and contrast, making it ideal for close-focus wide-angle work, while the NIKKOR Z 24–70mm f/2.8 S delivers the same high optical standard across a versatile focal range. Just as importantly, these lenses match beautifully in colour, contrast and rendering, allowing footage from different focal lengths to cut together seamlessly. The 70–180mm Micro remains one of the most unique lenses ever produced. Even after decades, I have not found another lens that combines its macro capability, working distance, and flexibility so effectively underwater. It allows me to frame delicate marine life without disturbing natural behaviour. The specialist optics — the Laowa Probe, Canon MP-E 65, and Infinity InfiniProbe ROBUSTO —extend that visual language even further. They reveal hidden worlds and perspectives that conventional lenses simply cannot achieve, while maintaining the image quality expected for premium natural history productions. I have invested in these lenses because I trust them completely. They deliver exceptional optical performance, reliable colour reproduction, and a consistent cinematic look across an enormous range of subject sizes. That consistency is essential when telling stories that move from sweeping underwater landscapes to the finest microscopic details. They are proven professional tools that continue to meet the demanding standards required for landmark wildlife films. — Doug Anderson DPs: Scott Duncan, Peter Wery, Russ Fill, Granger Scholtz, Christopher BarkerCategory: Outstanding Cinematography for a Reality Program Format: XAVC, ProResCameras: ALEXA 35, ALEXA Mini, DJI Drones, Freefly EMBER, Fujifilm Eterna Lenses: Angenieux, Canon, Fuji, Nikon, Zeiss, Mercury AtlasThe Look: “Survivor” celebrated 50 seasons this year, and we continue to cinematically elevate the storytelling. As the technology grows, we grow with it. We evolve the imagery: different angles, different lighting, different formats, expanding new ways of seeing, keeping it fresh and custom. Every camera and lens has a purpose in our storytelling. We test everything extensively, and the question is always… what can this tool give us that elevates the scene or story? It has to be functional, reliable, and most importantly, it has to add something to the visual language of “Survivor.” The Sony Z750, Alexa 35, Alexa Mini, Sony Fx6’s, Freely Ember, DJI Drones, and newly, the Fujifilm ETERNA 55, woven together in our final visual color grade. We get a diverse palette that provides maximum visual impact that gives us our brand identity. The Alexa 35 provides large cinematic scope, giving us the beauty and sense of being there, compared to the Freely Ember, teeny tiny, but robust shooting 1000 fps. Functionality all over the place for specialty slow motion. The Fx6 gives us 20,000 ISO matched with a large aperture lens, maximizing opportunities with night tribal campfire-lit scenes deep in the jungle. The Fuji Eterna 55 offers a large format sensor with a classic Fujifilm color space, giving us classic cinema motion picture film quality. Shooting Survivor is about being ready, using your instincts. You don’t get a second take. Having the right tools, knowing when to use them, and never overusing them… that’s how we continue to evolve the “Survivor” look. — Scott Duncan Dir: Tamara Kotevska; DP: Jean Dakar  Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program Format: 4K DCI, XAVC-ICameras: Sony FX6, DJI Mavic 3 Pro CineLenses: Sigma 24-70, Sigma 60-600The Look: The nature of a documentary, with wildlife as a central element, really narrowed my lens choice down to zoom lenses. On a technical level, the Sigma 60-600 not only offered a great range, it also delivered good autofocus performance, which allowed me to solely focus on framing storks in flight, during landing and take-off. Shooting this film entirely on two lenses took off the burden of carrying more equipment or relying on more crew, which gave the director and me more space to immerse ourselves in our subject’s world and gave us the liberty of focusing on the story. Intimacy was a crucial aspect in the visual storytelling. We wanted this film to look and feel as if the audience were part of our characters’ world (both human and avian). We spent a great deal of time developing a bond of trust with our subjects, which was shaped by a natural collaboration. This is ultimately what gave the film its unique look. Minimal, lightweight equipment not only brought me closer to my subjects by creating a space of intimacy, it also gave me the flexibility, speed, and creative freedom of crafting shots while responding instinctively to unfolding moments. — Jean Dakar Nominated Episode: “Le Marche” DP: Matt Ball  Category: Outstanding Cinematography For A Nonfiction ProgramFormat: UHD 16:9Cameras: Canon C500MK2 and Ronin 4D 6K Lenses: Canon Sumire prime lens setThe Look: The Canon C500 Mark 2 is a great documentary camera. It hits a real sweet spot for the kind of films we make. It has beautiful colour reproduction, is very flattering for skin tones, and handles highlights exceptionally well. We knew we’d be shooting in Italy throughout the spring and summer, often in the middle of the day, so having that latitude in bright sunlight was really important. It’s also incredibly adaptable. We can strip it right back if needed or fully rig it so it’s comfortable to use over long periods handheld. Just as importantly, it’s an extremely reliable camera. When you know you’re going to be working in the heat, whether that’s outside or in a busy restaurant kitchen with a small documentary crew, you need equipment you can trust to work all day without slowing you down, and this camera has always given me that confidence. We chose the Sumire lenses because of the way they render an image when wide open. They have a softer contrast and a gentle bloom around highlights that takes some of the clinical edge off modern digital cameras. The camera and lenses together produced an image that felt cinematic but still natural. The Ronin 4D was used for all of the walking shots. It’s a fantastic gimbal camera because it’s ready to go straight out of the box, so we don’t lose time rigging a separate camera onto a gimbal. It also lends itself really well to working with a small unit, allowing us to move quickly and stay unobtrusive, while the autofocus is incredibly reliable, even in bright sunlight. That meant we could concentrate and react to what was happening in the frame rather than constantly worrying about the focus being slightly out. — Matt Ball Nominated Episode: “Indy Streets” Dir: Robbie Countryman; DP: Chuck Ozeas Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour) Format: 4K. 2500 EI base. Rated at 1600 EICameras: Sony Venice Lenses: Panavision Primo 11:1 zoom // Fujinon 20-120, 14-35 zoomsThe Look: On “The Upshaws,” every scene starts with the same two questions: where is the light coming from, and how do I make it feel as natural as possible? Sitcoms move fast. We’re cross-shooting close-ups and center wides simultaneously, so it’s a balancing act. Whatever the source is for a given scene, whether it’s the windows, the practicals, or stage “sun,” I try to motivate the lighting as much as possible. The show is a comedy, but it also digs into real issues this family faces, so making the light feel honest is always the goal. I’d normally like to stay with one lens manufacturer, but this was a case of using the best tool for the job. Our wing cameras carry Panavision Primo 11:1s, which are slightly softer and warmer than our center cam glass, with a little falloff at the edges. That makes them ideal for close-ups. The center cams are on Fuji 20-120s, whose range lets us grab a wide and push into a single when needed. Since those are sharper edge-to-edge, I worked with David Dodson at Panavision Woodland Hills to detune them slightly, adding some focus falloff at the edges. — Chuck Ozeas Nominated Episode: “Do A Wrexham” DPs: Ed Edwards, Verdy Oliver, Tom Reece, Kieren StartupCategory: Outstanding Cinematography for a Reality ProgramFormat: X-OCN LTCameras: Venice, FX9, FX6, FX3Lenses: Angenieux EZ1 30-90mm, Zeiss Super Speeds, Canon CN20 50-1000mmThe Look: For us, it always comes back to being present in the story. The stories we film don’t wait for us, so we want the technical side of filmmaking to almost disappear once we’re in a scene. We’ve used the Sony Venice system for a long time and know it intimately. We trust the sensor; we know how far we can push it and, importantly, we’re not thinking about the camera when something meaningful starts to happen. A lot of our choices are really about how they allow us to behave around the people we’re filming. We’ll often work in Super 35 with an Angenieux 30–90mmm because that range lets us stay with a scene rather than interrupting it with lens changes. For football, a CN20 allows us to find very intimate human moments from a distance. Sometimes giving somebody space is the best way of getting close to them. If the crowd erupts, it’s a fun time to be in the mix with a wide lens, and we have great shooters strategically placed in the stadium for that. The same thinking carries into our interviews. Our show often uses large, symmetrical compositions, and the Zeiss Super Speeds give us enough separation and dimensionality to find intimacy within those wider frames without imposing too much style on the person. When the story requires us to be smaller and less visible, we’ll move to an FX6 and G Master zooms; the changing rooms come to mind here, where we’re normally shooting from the shower room through a door into the room. Ultimately, none of these choices are really about the equipment. They’re about removing barriers between us and the people we’re filming. If we’re thinking about the camera when the story is happening, we’ve probably chosen the wrong tool. — Leighton Cox Nominated Episode: “Our History” Dir: Ti West; DP: Christian Sprenger, ASC  Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour) Format: ARRIRAWCameras: ALEXA 265Lenses: Todd AO 65mm Spherical primesThe Look: Being a story that was from another time in history, I wanted to elevate the visual depth of this episode from the rest of the season. We shot ALEXA 35 (S35) for all of the present-day episodes, so changing the format, lenses, and aspect ratio, and into a mostly handheld perspective really shifted the feeling of the story while still maintaining the soul of the rest of the series. — Christian Sprenger Nominated Episode: “The End of Wondering” Dir: Margaret Brown; DPs: Christopher LaMarca, Justin Zweifach Category: Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program Format: Digital UHD XAVC-I, OCN-LTCameras: Sony BURANO, FX6, FX3Lenses: LEICA SUMMILUX-M, ANGENIEUX 37-102The Look: “The Yogurt Shop Murders” was initially released into the world as a four-part series with the case unsolved. But just one month after the fourth and final episode aired, and after 34 years, the Austin Police Department solved the case. Episode 5, “The End of Wondering,” had to reflect this seismic shift. For Episodes 1 through 4, we employed 4:3 interview framing and colored lighting to externalize emotions. Our idea in using 4:3, which matched the native ratio of the early ’90s archival, was to suggest the material was constrained by the past. We chose sharp, modern glass as a juxtaposition, seeking to remind viewers that this was indeed the present, and participants were still processing the inexplicable events of 1991. Expressive lighting, borrowed from ’50s melodrama, we hoped would subtly call attention to the imagery itself, the questionable process of externalizing trauma, and paint the true crime genre as part of the story. But then the case was solved. And with three days to determine an approach, we decided to drop the apparatus. Small cameras, available light, 1.78 framing for the present, limited crew – we wanted the episode to feel as though looking behind the veil of the series itself, and behind the mystery too. Logistically, the simple approach was better for keeping up with rapidly unfolding emotions and events, and also helped us cultivate an intimate environment with participants, less gear and fewer bodies in the room. We used the same lens family for continuity across the rupture in style, but we swapped the 50mm on A cam for a 35, as if allowing the frame to breathe a bit, and traded a prime for a zoom on B cam. Slow zooms quietly applied pressure to the frame as decades-held emotions bubbled over. The question that emerged once the case was solved was clear and simple: what does it mean to go from uncertainty to certainty? Our goal with the imagery was to keep it quiet and allow the answers to come through. — Justin Zweifach By providing your information, you agree to our Terms of Use and our Privacy Policy.

The full-back still does not know the extent of his physical condition; he will have to wait for the swelling in the area to go down so his knee can be examined. title: Cribbs Ringer v. Comal Independent School District - American Civil Liberties Union
content: Certiorati Briefing A petition for a writ of certiorari is a brief that asks the Supreme Court to review a lower court’s ruling, either from a federal appellate court or a state’s court of last resort. A Brief in Opposition urges the Court not to review the case, and is filed by the party that prevailed in the lower court. A group of Texas families are challenging a 2025 Texas law, S.B. 10, that requires public schools to conspicuously display a state-selected, Protestant version of the Ten Commandments in every classroom. Nearly 50 years ago, the Supreme Court overturned a similar Kentucky law because it violated the First Amendment. After an appellate court ruled that S.B. 10 does not violate the Constitution, the Baha’i, Christian, Jewish, Hindu, and nonreligious families involved in the lawsuit are asking the Supreme Court to hear their case and to block the law. The First Amendment prohibits states from forcing scripture on public-school students, and it guarantees families — not politicians or the government —the right to guide children’s religious belief and education. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. In 2025, Texas lawmakers enacted S.B. 10, which requires all public elementary and secondary schools to display a Protestant version of the Ten Commandments selected by the legislature. As mandated by the law, the displays must be at least 16 by 20 inches in size and must be hung in a “conspicuous place” in each classroom. The Ten Commandments must be written largely enough that students can see them no matter where they are seated. In other words, the displays are designed to be unavoidable for students. From kindergarten through twelfth grade, the government will impose this religious doctrine on children for nearly every hour they are in public school. A group of Texas families with children in public schools across the state filed a federal lawsuit challenging S.B. 10 in response to their school districts displaying or preparing to display Ten Commandments posters in classrooms despite a federal ruling that the state-mandated displays violate families’ religious freedom and the separation of church and state. The families suing in Cribbs Ringer v. Comal Independent School District are Jewish, Christian, Hindu, Baha’I, and nonreligious; some families include parents who are reverends. The families allege that forcing the Ten Commandments on their children in every classroom will pressure the children to conform to the state’s favored religious beliefs and interfere with parents’ right to guide their children’s religious instruction. In their lawsuit, the parents sought an injunction requiring their school districts to take down the displays and prohibiting them from posting new ones. The district court agreed, ruling that the Ten Commandments law likely violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Nearly 70 years of Supreme Court precedent back the district court’s ruling, including a milestone 1980 Supreme Court decision in a lawsuit brought by the ACLU that struck down a similar Kentucky Ten Commandments law. Nevertheless, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed the district court in April 2026. The appellate court upheld S.B. 10 and cleared the way for the Ten Commandments to be posted in the plaintiff children’s classrooms. Together with the families in a similar lawsuit challenging S.B. 10, Nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District, the families in Cribbs Ringer filed a petition for a writ of certiorari with the U.S. Supreme Court in August 2026. They have asked the Court to hear both cases, reverse the appellate court’s rulings, and protect their families’ religious freedom.
